  summary: `adapters.fs_local.LocalFs.append_line` wraps an `os.fsync` failure (occurring AFTER a successful `os.write`) into the same generic `FsError` message as a write failure, so a future caller that catches `FsError` and naively retries the whole append on ANY failure would duplicate an already-physically-written line -- fsync failing after a successful write is not equivalent to "nothing happened."
  evidence: Flagged during Story 3.1's adversarial review (Edge Case Hunter). Verified by code inspection: both `os.write`'s short-write path and `os.fsync`'s own `OSError` are caught by the same outer `except OSError as exc: raise FsError(...)`, with no field distinguishing "the write itself failed/was incomplete" from "the write succeeded but fsync did not." Not fixed in this story: no real caller retries on `FsError` yet (no CLI wiring exists -- see the CLI-wiring entry above), so this is a latent hazard for whichever future story (Story 3.3's launch, or Story 3.4's supervisor) builds retry logic around this primitive; that story must account for write-succeeded-fsync-failed as a distinct outcome, not invent a distinguishing signal unattended here with no real caller to validate the design against.

### DW-FU-3-2-8: `FoldResult`'s query surface cannot express the unit of unevaluability its own AC names. The AC says a bad line "makes its own STORY KEY and decision domain unevaluable", but `is_evaluable(story, None)` raises `ValueError` (the both-or-neither guard added in an earlier review pass), so the story-level question is illegal to ask and the per-`(story, kind)` answers do not compose without enumerating every `kind` in existence. The same pass's `for_story` type guard removed the only way to select the run-scoped (`story is None`) entries. And `by_kind`/`for_story` return a plain tuple indistinguishable from a complete answer when a quarantine dropped entries, with no in-band signal and nothing forcing the `is_evaluable` call -- against AD-8's "unevaluable is a failure, never silently dropped".

### DW-FU-3-2-9: The fold accepts, and the writer re-emits, the non-RFC-8259 bare literals `NaN`/`Infinity`/`-Infinity` -- Python's `json` parses them unless `parse_constant=` is supplied and `json.dumps` emits them unless `allow_nan=False`, so `JournalEntry.__post_init__`'s own serializability check passes them straight through. The journal is explicitly the cross-component source of truth, and such a line is unreadable by `jq`, Go, or Rust.

The journal is explicitly the cross-component source of truth, and such a line is unreadable by `jq`, Go, or Rust.
  evidence: Flagged during Story 3.2's third review pass (Blind Hunter). Verified live: a line with `"payload": {"x": NaN}` folds to `entries=1` with `payload={'x': nan}`, and `prepare_for_write` regenerates a line containing the bare token `NaN`. Not fixed in this story: a read-side-only fix (`parse_constant=`) would make Marshal quarantine lines Marshal itself wrote -- strictly worse -- so the coherent remedy also sets `allow_nan=False` on the WRITE side, which changes Story 3.1's shipped `JournalEntry` construction contract (a payload containing `float('nan')` would begin failing at construction) with its own tests and no AC asking for it.

This degrades gracefully under the architecture's OWN existing rules rather than corrupting anything -- AD-28 already says a lone open `intent` "stays open and is reported, never inferred closed", and AD-21's amendment (F-17) already classifies an unclosed intent `Verdict.WARN`, never `error`, specifically so it does not break exit-0 convergence -- so this is a real but bounded paper-trail gap, not a crash or false green. Not fixed in this story: the coherent remedy (wrap the spawn-through-outcome-write region so a `KeyboardInterrupt` during the poll still attempts a best-effort outcome write before re-raising, or shield the poll from interruption entirely) is a process-lifecycle-robustness design decision more naturally owned by Story 3.4's supervisor (which already deals with externally-observed process state) than a one-line patch here with no AC asking for it.

### DW-FU-3-3-4: `spin`'s bounded `harness_run_id` poll never asks whether the spawned child is still alive, so a `bmad-loop run` that launches and then exits within milliseconds -- most commonly on `cmd_run`'s own `verify.worktree_clean()` refusal, which returns 1 BEFORE printing its "run ... starting" line -- is reported as a successful detached launch: `MRS-SPIN-004` at WARN, exit 0, the dead pid journaled in the `outcome` entry, and the full poll window burned waiting for a line that can never arrive.

- source_spec: `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/spec-3-3-detached-launch-with-scoped-story-selection.md`
  summary: `spin`'s bounded `harness_run_id` poll never asks whether the spawned child is still alive, so a `bmad-loop run` that launches and then exits within milliseconds -- most commonly on `cmd_run`'s own `verify.worktree_clean()` refusal, which returns 1 BEFORE printing its "run ... starting" line -- is reported as a successful detached launch: `MRS-SPIN-004` at WARN, exit 0, the dead pid journaled in the `outcome` entry, and the full poll window burned waiting for a line that can never arrive.
  evidence: Flagged during Story 3.3's second review pass (Blind Hunter and Edge Case Hunter, independently, both verified live: a child exiting 1 after ~10 ms still costs the full 5.01 s window and yields `SpinResult(pid=..., harness_run_id=None)` -> exit 0). `_poll_for_harness_run_id(log_path)` never receives the `Popen` object, so a dead child is indistinguishable from a slow one, and the real error text sits unread in `harness.log`. A CI wrapper doing `marshal factory spin acme && echo launched` therefore reports success for a run that never began. NOT fixed in this pass because the story's contract covers this case and answers it deliberately the other way: its I/O matrix's `harness_run_id`-unconfirmed row (trigger: "the redirected log never shows the 'starting' line within the poll window") specifies exactly the current behaviour -- "spawn still counted a success (pid known)", exit 0, WARN -- consistent with `MRS-SPIN-003`'s own "raise only when the process could not be LAUNCHED at all", and the story's Never clause ("do not attach a supervisor -- `spin` launches and returns; nothing watches the process after this story") puts child-liveness inspection in Story 3.4's scope. Changing the verdict here would contradict the frozen contract; Story 3.4's supervisor, which already tracks process liveness, is the coherent owner -- alongside the two lifecycle items already logged above.

### DW-FU-3-3-6: `--foreground` bypasses the AD-38 feed-completeness gate entirely -- it returns from `run_spin` before `story_feed_error`/`story_feed_keys`/`resolve_feed` are ever called -- so a story feed containing a key that fails `core.identity.normalize` refuses the detached launch with `MRS-IDENT-001` but launches perfectly happily behind the flag, and the resulting run produces no Marshal run id and no journal entries at all.

- source_spec: `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/spec-3-3-detached-launch-with-scoped-story-selection.md`
  summary: `--foreground` bypasses the AD-38 feed-completeness gate entirely -- it returns from `run_spin` before `story_feed_error`/`story_feed_keys`/`resolve_feed` are ever called -- so a story feed containing a key that fails `core.identity.normalize` refuses the detached launch with `MRS-IDENT-001` but launches perfectly happily behind the flag, and the resulting run produces no Marshal run id and no journal entries at all.
  evidence: Flagged during Story 3.3's second review pass (Blind Hunter). Confirmed by reading `cli/spin.py::run_spin`: the `--foreground` branch sits between the loop-home gate and the story-feed gate, and its own module docstring documents the omission as deliberate ("skips the story-feed/journal machinery entirely -- there is no minted run id and nothing to journal for a launch that never called `spin`"). Real consequence: AD-38's completeness guarantee, and the journal's coverage of launches, are both conditional on a CLI flag, so a `--foreground` run that executes six stories is invisible to `core.journal.fold` -- the module Story 3.2 declared Marshal's ONE producer of accumulating run state. Not fixed in this pass: the spec's Always bullet defines `--foreground` purely as "calls a synchronous, stdio-inheriting HarnessPort path instead of the detached one and relays its exit code" and its order-of-operations bullet describes only the detached path, so whether a foreground run is a first-class journaled Marshal run (and what its envelope would even be, given the flag deliberately bypasses the envelope) is an unanswered design question, not a mechanical omission.

  summary: AC #2's "cannot be disabled, silenced, or reconfigured from inside the agent session" is enforced structurally only against IMPORT-shaped and IPC-shaped channels (the AD-9 import-linter contract plus the AST scans for `socket`/`multiprocessing`/`input()`/`sys.stdin`), but the run's own `journal.jsonl` is a shared file the agent session can write -- and every continuation decision the supervisor makes past its first read depends on that file, so the session can silence its own supervisor through it.
  evidence: Read live against `supervisor/__main__.py`: the one journal read at `run_supervisor`'s top decides attach-vs-inert, and every tick's continuation depends on `fs.append_line` succeeding (the `(FsError, ValueError)` branch prints one stderr line and returns 1). The agent session runs INSIDE the loop home and reaches the run directory through the Tier-3 backlink, so it holds write access. Two concrete paths: `chmod 0444 journal.jsonl` (or replacing it with a directory) makes the next tick fail and exit, leaving the journal byte-identical to a healthy supervisor mid-tick; corrupting the `run-launch` line before the sidecar's first read makes it exit inert forever. The module docstring's claim that the journal "is append-only, so its own future entries cannot be edited to control it" describes writer DISCIPLINE, not an enforced property of the file. Not fixed in this pass: every coherent remedy is privilege separation (a supervisor running as a different uid, an O_APPEND-only descriptor handed down from a more-privileged parent, or a second write target outside the session's reach) -- all of which contradict this story's own Always bullet that the supervisor's only write is the journal, and none of which any AC here asks for. The natural owner is whichever story first revisits AD-9's threat model as a whole rather than its import surface.

### DW-FU-3-5-6: `evaluate_idle` cannot distinguish "the session is genuinely idle" from "the observation channel itself is broken" -- two consecutive samples that are both `pane_content=None, log_mtime=None` are treated identically to two identical non-`None` readings, so a broken `tmux` install, a permissions issue, or a transiently-missing harness-log path masquerades as maximal idleness and can drive the full ladder (nudge/stop-and-retry/defer) against an actively-working, healthy session purely because the observability channel, not the session, failed.

  summary: `evaluate_idle` cannot distinguish "the session is genuinely idle" from "the observation channel itself is broken" -- two consecutive samples that are both `pane_content=None, log_mtime=None` are treated identically to two identical non-`None` readings, so a broken `tmux` install, a permissions issue, or a transiently-missing harness-log path masquerades as maximal idleness and can drive the full ladder (nudge/stop-and-retry/defer) against an actively-working, healthy session purely because the observability channel, not the session, failed.

The natural owner is whichever story next hardens the supervisor against its own port failures rather than the watched session's.

### DW-FU-3-5-9: The idle ladder's whole input signal is byte-identity of successive `tmux capture-pane` outputs, so ANY continuously-redrawing pane element in the agent CLI being supervised -- an elapsed-seconds counter, a spinner, a live token tally -- makes `current.pane_content != previous.pane_content` true on every single tick even while the agent is genuinely hung on a stalled tool call, and the ladder can never leave `LadderRung.NONE`. FR-12 would then be silently inert against exactly the wedged-session class it exists to catch.

- source_spec: `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/spec-3-5-idle-strand-detection.md`
  summary: The idle ladder's whole input signal is byte-identity of successive `tmux capture-pane` outputs, so ANY continuously-redrawing pane element in the agent CLI being supervised -- an elapsed-seconds counter, a spinner, a live token tally -- makes `current.pane_content != previous.pane_content` true on every single tick even while the agent is genuinely hung on a stalled tool call, and the ladder can never leave `LadderRung.NONE`. FR-12 would then be silently inert against exactly the wedged-session class it exists to catch.
  evidence: Read live against `core/supervise.py::idle_since`/`evaluate_idle`: the fresh-output test is a raw `!=` over the whole captured pane string, OR-ed with the log mtime, so the NOISIEST of the two signals always wins and a single changing character re-arms the window. Not fixed in this pass: the OR semantics are mandated verbatim by this story's own Always bullet ("Fresh output (pane content OR mtime changed since the previous sample) re-arms the window"), so narrowing it -- to a normalized/stripped comparison, a similarity threshold, an AND over both signals, or a diff that ignores a trailing status line -- is a contract change to the decision core, not a mechanical patch. Whether it bites at all depends on what the supervised agent CLI actually renders, which no test here can determine; the natural owner is the first story that observes a real wedged run failing to escalate, or a deliberate hardening pass over the pane-diff signal itself.

### DW-FU-3-5-10: `adapters/observer_mux.py::_resolve_window` targets whichever window `tmux` marks ACTIVE in the session, which is the engine's window in the ordinary case but is re-pointed by any human who attaches (`marshal factory attach` / `tmux attach`) and switches windows to inspect something. From that moment the supervisor samples the WRONG pane -- so idle time accrues against a window the engine never writes to, and a firing `nudge` types its text into the operator's own pane instead of the agent's.

- source_spec: `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/spec-3-5-idle-strand-detection.md`
  summary: `adapters/observer_mux.py::_resolve_window` targets whichever window `tmux` marks ACTIVE in the session, which is the engine's window in the ordinary case but is re-pointed by any human who attaches (`marshal factory attach` / `tmux attach`) and switches windows to inspect something. From that moment the supervisor samples the WRONG pane -- so idle time accrues against a window the engine never writes to, and a firing `nudge` types its text into the operator's own pane instead of the agent's.
  evidence: Read live against `_resolve_window`: it parses `tmux list-windows -F '#{window_id}\t#{window_active}'` and accepts the single row whose `window_active` is `1`, with a docstring that justifies this as "a session always has exactly one active window" -- true, but which window that IS is operator-mutable state, not a property of the engine. Partially mitigated in this pass: `_NUDGE_TEXT` was stripped of every shell metacharacter, so a nudge landing in a shell pane now costs one "command not found" line rather than executing a fragment and hanging the shell at a `>` continuation prompt. Not fixed: targeting the engine's own window specifically would require a durable identifier for it, and this story's own Design Notes record that the window id is backend-assigned at creation and persisted nowhere Marshal can read it back from (confirmed by grepping a live `state.json`/`journal.jsonl` for `window_id`/`native_id`). The natural owner is whichever story can either establish a window-naming convention with the harness upstream or persist the engine's window id at launch.

### DW-FU-3-5-11: `adapters/harness_bmadloop.py::stop` runs `bmad-loop stop` with `capture_output=True` and then discards both captured streams, using only `returncode`. So the worst case this whole story exists to prevent -- the terminal `defer` rung's stop not taking, the supervisor exiting, and the wedged run continuing to burn tokens unsupervised -- is reported as `MRS-SUPV-002` "bmad-loop reported it was not stopped" with no cause attached, even though `bmad-loop` printed one to stderr and this adapter read it.

- source_spec: `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/spec-3-5-idle-strand-detection.md`
  summary: `adapters/harness_bmadloop.py::stop` runs `bmad-loop stop` with `capture_output=True` and then discards both captured streams, using only `returncode`. So the worst case this whole story exists to prevent -- the terminal `defer` rung's stop not taking, the supervisor exiting, and the wedged run continuing to burn tokens unsupervised -- is reported as `MRS-SUPV-002` "bmad-loop reported it was not stopped" with no cause attached, even though `bmad-loop` printed one to stderr and this adapter read it.
  evidence: Read live against `harness_bmadloop.py::stop`: `result = subprocess.run([...], capture_output=True, ...)` followed by `return result.returncode == 0` -- `result.stdout`/`result.stderr` are never read, and no logger exists in this adapter to route them to. Confirmed the consumer side too: both `MRS-SUPV-002` construction sites in `supervisor/__main__.py` can only interpolate what `stop()` gives back, which for the non-raising path is a bare `False`. Not fixed in this pass: surfacing the cause requires widening `HarnessPort.stop`'s own return contract beyond `bool` (a result object, or an exception carrying stderr on the non-launch-failure path), which changes the documented raise/return split every other method on this port shares -- a port-shape decision, not a mechanical patch, and no AC here asks for it. The natural owner is whichever story first needs machine-readable harness failure detail (Story 3.7's FR-16 deferral capture is the obvious candidate, since a reason-class taxonomy needs exactly this).

### DW-FU-3-6-5: The usage-staleness gate in `supervisor/__main__.py` computes `moment.timestamp() - state_mtime`, a WALL-CLOCK delta, to decide whether `state.json` is fresh -- while every other elapsed-time decision in the same tick loop deliberately uses `clock.monotonic()`, with a dedicated regression test (`test_a_wall_clock_jump_never_escalates_the_ladder`) pinning that discipline for the idle ladder.

- source_spec: `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/spec-3-6-budget-ceilings-and-the-heaviest-story-advisory.md`
  summary: The usage-staleness gate in `supervisor/__main__.py` computes `moment.timestamp() - state_mtime`, a WALL-CLOCK delta, to decide whether `state.json` is fresh -- while every other elapsed-time decision in the same tick loop deliberately uses `clock.monotonic()`, with a dedicated regression test (`test_a_wall_clock_jump_never_escalates_the_ladder`) pinning that discipline for the idle ladder.
  evidence: Reviewer-identified independently by both lenses in review pass 2, read live against the gate at `supervisor/__main__.py` (the `is_stale` expression) and against `ports/clock.py::monotonic`'s own rationale. Consequence in both directions: a forward NTP step or a suspend/resume marks a genuinely fresh sample stale, so both token ceilings go dark and a spurious `MRS-SUPV-006` fires; a backward step marks a stale sample fresh, so a breach decision -- a hard `harness.stop` -- is taken on exactly the evidence the gate exists to reject. Not fixed in review pass 2: a filesystem mtime IS a wall-clock quantity, so there is no direct monotonic comparison available; making this sound needs either a monotonic-anchored cross-check (remember the mtime and monotonic reading from the previous tick and require both to agree) or an explicit "the clock moved non-monotonically, treat this tick's sample as unevaluable" branch. That is a design decision about the freshness model, not a mechanical patch. The natural owner is whichever story next revisits the staleness model -- see the sibling entry about `state.json`'s save cadence, which wants the same rework.

### DW-FU-3-6-6: Both token ceilings are structurally dark for most of a long session. bmad-loop only rewrites `state.json` at session boundaries, but the staleness window reuses `idle_threshold_minutes` (default 25 min), so from minute 25 of a session onward every sample is classified `stale-evidence`, both token ceilings are skipped, and a `MRS-SUPV-006` WARN is journaled on healthy long-running stories.

- source_spec: `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/spec-3-6-budget-ceilings-and-the-heaviest-story-advisory.md`
  summary: Both token ceilings are structurally dark for most of a long session. bmad-loop only rewrites `state.json` at session boundaries, but the staleness window reuses `idle_threshold_minutes` (default 25 min), so from minute 25 of a session onward every sample is classified `stale-evidence`, both token ceilings are skipped, and a `MRS-SUPV-006` WARN is journaled on healthy long-running stories.
  evidence: Reviewer-identified independently by both lenses in review pass 2 and measured against this machine's live journals: inter-write gaps of 178.8, 107.1, 93.7, 71.6, 56.6, 52.7 and 39.6 minutes were observed within single runs, against a 25-minute staleness window -- and this repo's own rendered harness policy sets `session_timeout_min = 180`, so a single dev session can legitimately leave `state.json` untouched for three hours. Net effect: the token ceilings can only ever act one tick after a phase boundary, i.e. after a session has already spent its tokens, never during the runaway session they exist to bound. The acceptance criterion "a wedged session's frozen counter can never defeat the ceiling" is therefore satisfied by the wall-clock half alone, exactly as AD-32 intends -- so this is a reach-of-enforcement gap, not a correctness break. Not fixed in review pass 2: the fix is to give usage-staleness its own basis (e.g. `max(idle_threshold_s, session_timeout_s)`) or to treat an unchanged-but-consistent sample as usable rather than skipping, both of which change the semantics AD-32's F-24 amendment fixed in place. The natural owner is whichever story revisits the freshness model; pair it with the monotonic-basis entry above.

### DW-FU-3-6-8: A per-STORY ceiling breach terminates the whole RUN. `harness.stop(home, harness_run_id)` stops the entire bmad-loop run and the tick loop then exits, so one outlier story breaching `max_tokens_per_story` or `max_wall_clock_minutes_per_story` abandons every remaining story in an overnight wave -- and the detach reason names a story-scoped ceiling for a run-terminating action.

  summary: A per-STORY ceiling breach terminates the whole RUN. `harness.stop(home, harness_run_id)` stops the entire bmad-loop run and the tick loop then exits, so one outlier story breaching `max_tokens_per_story` or `max_wall_clock_minutes_per_story` abandons every remaining story in an overnight wave -- and the detach reason names a story-scoped ceiling for a run-terminating action.
  evidence: Reviewer-identified (Blind Hunter, review pass 2), read live against `_act_on_budget_transition` and `HarnessPort.stop`'s own contract. This is spec-sanctioned today: the intent contract's own Always bullet says a BREACH of either scope mirrors the idle ladder's terminal `defer` and exits via `supervisor-detach`, and its Never bullet rules out `stop-and-retry` for any budget breach. The rationale given there ("retrying the same story/run would immediately re-hit the same ceiling") justifies not retrying the offending story; it does not by itself justify killing the innocent remainder of the wave. Nothing marks the offending story as deferred in bmad-loop's own state either, so a re-launch simply re-runs it. Not fixed in review pass 2: a defer-this-story-and-continue path needs a harness capability Marshal does not have today (bmad-loop exposes run-level stop, not story-level skip) plus an amendment to this story's own intent contract -- a contract-level decision, out of scope for a review patch. The natural owner is whichever story first needs per-story deferral, most plausibly the FR-16 deferral-capture work.

By contrast `task.sessions` and `task.tokens` are never reassigned anywhere in `runs.py`/`engine.py` -- they accumulate across attempts and survive the re-arm -- and `task.tokens` is already parsed by `adapters/harness_bmadloop.py::usage_snapshot` and is literally the budget quantity the advisory exists to predict. The mechanism itself works (across 30 real runs, `attempt >= 2` appears 10x and `deferred`/`escalated` 11x); it just reads the mutable field rather than the durable one. Not fixed in review pass 3: the intent contract names `attempt >= 2` and the terminal phases explicitly, so switching the input is a contract-level change, not a patch. Pair it with the spec-size entry above -- one decision about what FR-14 should actually predict from covers both.

This is a second-order consequence of review pass 1's own (correct) fix for the opposite defect: a single transient read failure used to reset the per-story clock for a story that was still running, so the carry-forward rule became "only a POSITIVE reading ever changes `current_story_key`". That rule has no staleness bound of its own -- unlike the token path, which at least gates on mtime -- so an unreadable `state.json` that never heals (a permissions change, a truncated write) leaves the per-story wall-clock ceiling consuming a stale `story_started_monotonic` unconditionally. The only diagnostic is the same `MRS-SUPV-006` WARN already firing for the read failure itself. Low likelihood, and the run-scope wall-clock ceiling bounds the damage. Not fixed in review pass 3: bounding the carry-forward needs a "how long may a story attribution outlive its last confirmation?" decision that belongs with the freshness-model rework, and a naive bound would reintroduce exactly the defect pass 1 fixed.

### DW-FU-3-7-5: `marshal factory resume` still reports success (exit 0, a pid, a journaled `run-resume` OUTCOME, a fresh supervisor) when the run is still LIVE, because `HarnessPort.resume` detaches and the child's exit code is never observed -- `bmad-loop resume` itself refuses a provably-live engine ("resuming would double-drive it; stop it first", exit 1) only AFTER the process has started.

- source_spec: `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/spec-3-7-escalation-deferral-and-resume.md`
  summary: `marshal factory resume` still reports success (exit 0, a pid, a journaled `run-resume` OUTCOME, a fresh supervisor) when the run is still LIVE, because `HarnessPort.resume` detaches and the child's exit code is never observed -- `bmad-loop resume` itself refuses a provably-live engine ("resuming would double-drive it; stop it first", exit 1) only AFTER the process has started.
  evidence: Reviewer-identified (Blind Hunter, review pass 2), confirmed live against the installed `bmad_loop` 0.9.0's `cli.py::cmd_resume`, which gates on `runs.engine_liveness(run_dir) == "alive"` and returns 1 post-start. The sibling `state.finished` case WAS fixed in this pass (`RunStatusSnapshot.finished` + an `MRS-SPIN-011` refusal before any spawn), because bmad-loop's answer there is a plain durable flag Marshal can read from the same `state.json` it already reads. Liveness is not: it requires probing `engine.pid`, which has no `HarnessPort` counterpart and no Marshal-side primitive, and pid-liveness carries its own three-valued (`alive`/`dead`/`unknown`) semantics that would need a policy decision about what Marshal does with `unknown`. Blast radius is bounded -- bmad-loop's own refusal means no double-drive ever actually happens; the damage is a junk run directory plus a `run-resume` entry in an append-only EVIDENCE journal recording a resume that did not take. The same detached-launch blind spot is pre-existing and structural (`run_spin` has had it since Story 3.3, mitigated only by `MRS-SPIN-004`'s post-launch `harness_run_id` poll); the natural owner is whichever future story adds a general "confirm the detached child was accepted" primitive, which `supervisor/__main__.py::retry_verify_pending` already prototypes for the stop-and-retry path alone.

### DW-FU-3-8-2: `VcsPort.push`'s upstream-configured path parses `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref <branch>@{upstream}`'s own `<remote>/<remote_branch>` output by splitting on the FIRST `/` -- a remote name containing a `/` (not possible for a plain `git remote add <name> <url>`-created remote, whose name is validated by git itself, but theoretically reachable via a hand-edited `.git/config`) would misparse. Not fixed: no real caller in this codebase names a remote with a `/`, and refusing to guess (the `VcsCommandError` this method already raises when the split yields an empty remote or branch half) is the correct behavior for the input this method's own contract expects.

### DW-FU-3-8-3: The durability interval-push watcher's clock baseline (`last_durability_push_monotonic`) is process-local and reset on every supervisor restart/reattach, never reconciled against the journal's own last `"stage-push"` entry -- so the advertised "floor" guarantee (a push at least every N minutes) is not actually durable across a crash-and-reattach cycle. A supervisor that crashes 1 second before the interval was due to fire, then reattaches, restarts the clock from zero and can go a further full interval before its next unconditional push, silently doubling the worst-case gap the floor is supposed to bound.

### DW-FU-4-2-2: `deploy recover-spec`'s epics-derived fallback checks whether its target file already exists (`fs.exists(dest)`), and only then writes it -- a check-then-act race, not an atomic exclusive create. Two concurrent `recover-spec` invocations for the same slug/key could both pass the existence check before either writes, and the second write would silently overwrite the first's content, violating the command's own "never overwrite an existing file" guarantee.

- source_spec: `_bmad-output/projects/pyforge-marshal/implementation-artifacts/spec-4-2-teardown-reachability-and-spec-recovery-assistance.md`
  summary: `deploy recover-spec`'s epics-derived fallback checks whether its target file already exists (`fs.exists(dest)`), and only then writes it -- a check-then-act race, not an atomic exclusive create. Two concurrent `recover-spec` invocations for the same slug/key could both pass the existence check before either writes, and the second write would silently overwrite the first's content, violating the command's own "never overwrite an existing file" guarantee.
  evidence: Code review pass on Story 4.2 (Blind Hunter, D2). Confirmed by code inspection: `cli/deploy.py::run_recover_spec` calls `fs.exists(dest)` then, only in a later statement, `fs.write_text_atomic(dest, content)` -- the "atomic" in that method's name covers the WRITE itself (no partial/torn file), not the existence check preceding it. Low practical risk: this is a single-operator CLI with no concurrent-invocation use case documented anywhere in this project's own architecture, and `FsPort` has no exclusive-create primitive (`create_dir_exclusive` exists for directories, per `cli/init.py::_journal_abandonments`'s own use, but no file-level equivalent) to build a real fix on without growing the port's surface. Not fixed in this pass; the natural owner is whichever future story needs a genuinely concurrent-safe write path, at which point `FsPort` would need a `write_text_exclusive` (or similar) primitive first.

### DW-FU-4-14-7: `Path.glob` silently yields a PARTIAL result when an intermediate directory is unreadable, so `_gather_failed_patches` can miss a genuinely unlanded `changes.patch` that is present on disk -- reporting no entry and no finding, the exact silent-loss failure mode this durability signal exists to prevent.

- source_spec: `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/spec-4-14-the-failed-story-safety-net-is-reported.md`
  summary: `Path.glob` silently yields a PARTIAL result when an intermediate directory is unreadable, so `_gather_failed_patches` can miss a genuinely unlanded `changes.patch` that is present on disk -- reporting no entry and no finding, the exact silent-loss failure mode this durability signal exists to prevent.
  evidence: Review pass 3 (Blind Hunter; Edge Case Hunter reached the same mechanism from the symlink/permission angle). Verified against CPython 3.14.6 directly, not inferred: with two story dirs each holding a `changes.patch` and one of them `chmod 000`, `home.glob(".bmad-loop/runs/*/failed/*/changes.patch")` returns only the readable one and raises nothing -- `glob` swallows the `PermissionError` from `os.scandir` on intermediate segments -- so the helper's own `except OSError: return ()` guard never fires and the caller cannot tell a truncated enumeration from a complete one. Not fixed in this pass: every honest fix needs a way to REPORT the incomplete enumeration (manual `os.scandir` walk collecting per-directory errors, surfaced under a new `MRS-STATUS-*` code), since the two available silent behaviours -- partial result, or degrading the whole home to "none found" -- are both false greens; adding a third finding code and its registration/verdict/test surface is out of proportion to a read-only reporting story that pass 2 already reverted once. Low practical likelihood: these directories are created by bmad-loop itself, owned by the invoking user, and broken permissions inside a loop home would already be failing much of the harness. `core/status.py::FleetHomeFacts.failed_patches`'s docstring was corrected in pass 3 to stop claiming this field has "no could-not-be-consulted case of its own", so the limit is at least documented where a maintainer will read it.

### DW-FU-7-4-3: `load_manifest` applies the `since`/`until` filter irreversibly — it exposes no `at_version=` parameter and keeps no unfiltered copy — while its own module docstring tells every later story to trust its output "rather than re-parsing YAML itself", so a consumer needing entries outside the bundled model version has no sanctioned way to get them.

- source_spec: `_bmad-output/projects/pyforge-marshal/implementation-artifacts/spec-7-4-manifest-schema-loader-and-model-version-ranges.md`
  summary: `load_manifest` applies the `since`/`until` filter irreversibly — it exposes no `at_version=` parameter and keeps no unfiltered copy — while its own module docstring tells every later story to trust its output "rather than re-parsing YAML itself", so a consumer needing entries outside the bundled model version has no sanctioned way to get them.
  evidence: Follow-up review pass (Blind Hunter #2). Verified by code inspection (`load_manifest`'s closing `filtered_entries` comprehension is the only thing reaching the returned `Manifest`) and by reading AD-62, which specifies that the migration runner "selects the ordered chain from `state.model_version` to the bundled model version" — i.e. it reasons across a version RANGE, whereas the loader only ever answers for a single point. Severity is genuinely uncertain and that is why this is recorded rather than fixed: AD-62 registers migrations as `from_version`/`to_version` pure functions (code, not manifest entries), so a migration can encode what it needs about a retired artifact itself, and the need may never materialize. The append-only-ledger rationale this story documents is nonetheless preserved in the FILE and discarded at the API boundary. The fix, if wanted, is purely additive and non-breaking (an `at_version: ModelVersion | None = None` parameter, or an `all_entries` field alongside `entries`) and should be made by the story that first needs it, not speculatively here.

  summary: The `**/planning-artifacts/**` and `**/implementation-artifacts/**` never-write patterns never match the DIRECTORY node itself -- including `_bmad-output/planning-artifacts`, the exact path AD-61 names as its worked example of why symlink resolution matters -- so a directory-level operation (rmtree, rename, symlink re-point) on the Tier-2/Tier-3 tree passes the guard.

Verified by execution against the shipped 7-pattern list in both plausible matcher dialects: `_bmad-output/projects/foo/planning-artifacts/PRD.md` matches under `fnmatch` AND `PurePosixPath.match`, but `_bmad-output/projects/foo/planning-artifacts` and `_bmad-output/planning-artifacts` match under NEITHER -- the trailing `/**` requires at least one following segment. AD-61 (architecture.md:1076-1085) says "`fs` holds an immutable `NeverWrite` set (loaded from the manifest ...).   summary: Two REFERENCED ids (`bmad-installed-skills`, `bmad-skill-forge`) name no package that exists anywhere, because they label content `bmad-method install` delivers rather than a dependency -- yet `id` is the only handle FR-95's presence/floor probe has, so both will report as permanently-missing dependencies in every adopting repo.

Not fixed here: the classification is the PRD's and the companion doc's own ("via `bmad-method install`", REFERENCED), and distinguishing package-backed entries from installer-delivered ones needs a schema field (`package:`, or a `probe: none` marker) that Story 7.4's schema does not have -- outside this story's `manifest.yaml`+`artifact.py` Surface. Belongs with S-11.5, which implements the probe.

  summary: `<top>` is the sole anchor for the `model-ignores` and `model-badge` regions, but no file contains a line beginning `<top>` and no story defines sentinel semantics for it -- so under AD-56's stated fallback both regions append at end-of-file, putting the README badge at the bottom of every adopting repo's README.
  evidence: Second follow-up review pass (Edge Case Hunter + Blind Hunter, independent duplicates). Verified by execution: `<top>` line-prefix-matches at zero positions in the live `.gitignore` and `README.md`, while all five non-`<top>` anchors resolve correctly (AGENTS.md:29/49/63, CLAUDE.md:39/83). AD-56 (architecture.md:1028-1038) defines anchors as "literal line-prefix matchers" and specifies "insertion goes after the first match; if none matches, the region is appended at end of file" -- `<top>` appears in AD-56 only as an ordinary element of an illustrative list (`["## The tiers", "# CLAUDE.md", "<top>"]`), which implies a sentinel but states no semantics, and `Region.__post_init__` validates only non-blankness. Both affected regions are single-anchor, so there is no fallback behind them. The failure is silently non-fatal: a badge whose entire purpose is top-of-file placement lands last, and the `.gitignore` model block lands after any repo `!negation` rules that were written to win. Not fixed here: the two anchors are pinned verbatim by this story's Boundaries and `test_every_hybrid_region_declares_its_exact_anchor` asserts them, so the resolution is to define `<top>` in AD-56/S-8.1's grammar (or replace it with a real anchor) -- an architecture decision outside this story's data-only Surface.

### DW-FU-7-5-9: `specs-dir-legacy` is `applies_to: adopt`, i.e. EVERY adopt -- but the PRD scopes that directory to "`docs/specs/` only when legacy" and the entry's own rationale asserts the condition, so adopting a repo that never carried Tier-1 materialises the deprecated directory the model is phasing out.

- source_spec: `_bmad-output/projects/pyforge-marshal/implementation-artifacts/spec-7-5-the-v1-extraction-manifest.md`
  summary: `specs-dir-legacy` is `applies_to: adopt`, i.e. EVERY adopt -- but the PRD scopes that directory to "`docs/specs/` only when legacy" and the entry's own rationale asserts the condition, so adopting a repo that never carried Tier-1 materialises the deprecated directory the model is phasing out.
  evidence: Second follow-up review pass (Edge Case Hunter). Verified: the entry's rationale reads "legacy Tier-1 skeleton, created only when adopting a repo that already carries the legacy convention -- a fresh init never creates it", and the PRD's GENERATED-DERIVED table row reads "Directory skeletons (`docs/dreams/`, `docs/specs/` **only when legacy**, project subtrees)". `AppliesTo` has exactly three members (`INIT`/`ADOPT`/`BOTH`, `manifest.py:91-96`) and `_ENTRY_KEYS` carries no conditional-existence field, so the schema cannot express "only if the path already exists" -- `applies_to: adopt` means unconditional adopt. `test_applies_to_scoping_matches_the_spec` pins the id sets and cannot see the condition. The template body this story ships states the consequence itself (`templates/files/tiers.md.j2`: Tier 1 is "superseded by Tier 2; author no new files here"). S-10.7's AC ("Given an empty target directory") is the acceptance test that hits it. Not fixed here: the anchors and the heading-less body convention are both pinned by this story's Boundaries and Design Notes, and the resolution -- either host-file seed templates or an AD-56 "create with scaffold" branch -- belongs to the insertion story (S-8.4) and its architecture decision, not to this story's data-only Surface.

### DW-FU-7-6: Two Copier mechanism facts, discovered empirically during this spike, are hard requirements `seed/engine/copier.py` (Story 10.1) must satisfy and are not obvious from reading AD-52/A-04/FR-120 alone -- (a) Copier never auto-generates the answers file; the template package must ship a literal `{{ _copier_conf.answers_file }}.jinja` file (recommended body: `{{ _copier_answers|to_nice_yaml -}}`) or `.marshal/.copier-answers.yml` is simply never written, on any verb; (b) `run_update` must be passed `answers_file=".marshal/.copier-answers.yml"` explicitly on every call -- it does not auto-discover it from the template's `_answers_file` setting because the destination's existing subproject is resolved before the template is known, and omitting the argument raises `TypeError: Template not found`. `run_recopy` shares `run_update`'s exact `answers_file` parameter and dst-first resolution shape, so (b) almost certainly applies there too, but this was NOT independently exercised -- only `run_copy` and `run_update` were tested.

- source_spec: `_bmad-output/projects/pyforge-marshal/implementation-artifacts/spec-7-6-spike-0-copier-api-fit.md`
  summary: Two Copier mechanism facts, discovered empirically during this spike, are hard requirements `seed/engine/copier.py` (Story 10.1) must satisfy and are not obvious from reading AD-52/A-04/FR-120 alone -- (a) Copier never auto-generates the answers file; the template package must ship a literal `{{ _copier_conf.answers_file }}.jinja` file (recommended body: `{{ _copier_answers|to_nice_yaml -}}`) or `.marshal/.copier-answers.yml` is simply never written, on any verb; (b) `run_update` must be passed `answers_file=".marshal/.copier-answers.yml"` explicitly on every call -- it does not auto-discover it from the template's `_answers_file` setting because the destination's existing subproject is resolved before the template is known, and omitting the argument raises `TypeError: Template not found`. `run_recopy` shares `run_update`'s exact `answers_file` parameter and dst-first resolution shape, so (b) almost certainly applies there too, but this was NOT independently exercised -- only `run_copy` and `run_update` were tested.
  evidence: Verified empirically during Story 7.6's spike against a throwaway git-backed template and destination repos under the OS scratch directory, exercised via `copier==9.17.0`'s public API only (`run_copy`, `run_update`; `run_recopy` was not exercised -- see the summary's caveat, added on review since the first draft of this entry overstated (b) as covering `run_recopy` too). Finding (a): with no `{{ _copier_conf.answers_file }}.jinja` file in the template, `run_copy` never wrote the configured `.marshal/.copier-answers.yml`, on any verb tested; adding the file made it appear, confirmed both directions. Finding (b) is reproducible: omitting `answers_file=` on `run_update` reliably fails with `TypeError: Template not found` even when the answers file already exists on disk at the configured path; passing it explicitly resolves cleanly. Both are also recorded in the spike's own report (`_bmad-output/planning-artifacts/spike-0-copier-api-fit-report.md`) and in spec-7-6's Design Notes. Not fixed here: `seed/engine/copier.py` does not exist yet -- it is Story 10.1's Surface, gated by this spike's verdict (all five Spike-0 ACs PASS), not built by it; this entry ensures S-10.1 inherits the two mechanism requirements (plus the `run_recopy` open question) rather than rediscovering them the hard way.

### DW-FU-7-6-2: Four scenarios adjacent to Spike-0's five ACs were not exercised by this story's investigation -- each is beyond what the epics AC literally requires, but each is a plausible edge case for whoever hardens `seed/engine/copier.py` (S-10.1) or its tests: (1) `pretend=True` against a non-empty (update-style) destination, not just an empty one; (2) a `skip_if_exists`-listed path that does NOT yet exist in the destination (first `init`), to confirm normal creation rather than an accidental skip; (3) a required template variable with no default, omitted from `data=`, under closed stdin, to confirm a clean error rather than a hang; (4) a malformed or non-PEP-440-parseable git tag alongside well-formed ones, to confirm `run_update`'s tag resolution skips or errors predictably rather than misordering.

### DW-FU-2-8-2: Story 2.8 shipped only the pure `core/gate.py::classify_review_tier`/`resolve_review_cycles` mechanism plus its unit-tested proof, per the spec's own explicit Never clause (surface: `core/gate.py` alone, mirroring Story 2.4's `classify_doc_only_declaration` mechanism-only precedent). Three concrete pieces of follow-up wiring remain open, the same three Story 2.4 named for its own sibling mechanism, scoped here to review-tier classification: (1) no producer of `declared_low_risk`/`changed_files` exists ANYWHERE in the codebase yet -- no CLI flag, no story-spec-frontmatter field (`spec-template.md` has no `low_risk:`-shaped key), and no `VcsPort` call computes a real `changed_files` diff tuple; (2) nothing in `cli/gate.py` calls either new function, so `marshal gate evaluate` cannot classify a real story's review tier or bound its cycle allowance end-to-end; (3) "the classification is recorded in the run record" (AC2) is satisfied today ONLY via the returned `report` dict a future caller could fold into its own output, not a real write. Point (3) is a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT, more consequential gap than Story 2.4's own identical-sounding note: when Story 2.4 shipped, no journal existed anywhere in this package (`core/journal.py` was Epic 3/Story 3.1, still `backlog`), so "no real record" was the only possible state. A real journal now exists and is a live end-to-end caller (Story 3.1's `mint_run_id`/`append_line`, wired into `cli/spin.py::run_spin` by Story 3.3) -- so this story's classification facts have a durable home ready to receive them and simply are not routed there, rather than having nowhere to go at all.

### DW-FU-8-5-2: The seed-state schema's `opted_out` grammar is stricter than its own `managed[].id` grammar, so a legally-named artifact can be impossible to opt out of.

- source_spec: `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/spec-8-5-marker-deletion-as-a-sanctioned-opt-out.md`
  summary: The seed-state schema's `opted_out` grammar is stricter than its own `managed[].id` grammar, so a legally-named artifact can be impossible to opt out of.
  evidence: station-unresolved: see the previous entry's note -- the active-project env var disagreed with this file's own resolved project directory, forcing the unknown-station id shape. Blind Hunter, review pass 1. PRE-EXISTING, shipped by S-10.2, merely made observable by this story's first consumer of the field. `seed/state/schema.json` types `managed[].id` as `nonBlankString` (`"pattern": "\\S"`, so whitespace and `#` are both legal) while `opted_out`'s item pattern is `^[^\s#]+#[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*(?![\s\S])`. The schema's own description for `opted_out` asserts the artifact half is "deliberately as permissive as `managed[].id`" because "a stricter grammar here would make a legally-named entry's opt-out UNREPRESENTABLE" -- it is strictly less permissive, and that is exactly what happens. `ManifestEntry` requires only a non-blank `id`, so `record_opt_out(state, "has a space", "tiers")` raises rather than recording. NOT fixed in this pass: the fix is a `schema.json` change, which this story's Never bullets explicitly forbid (no new key, no schema edit, no state-schema migration), and it needs a decision about which of the two grammars moves -- tighten `managed[].id` to a slug (breaking existing state) or widen `opted_out`'s artifact half (weakening the key's parseability at the `#` separator). Not reachable with any manifest id in the fleet today; every real id is a slug.

### DW-FU-8-5-4: `clear_opt_out` drops a live `managed[]` claim when handed a region that is still PRESENT in the file, and no caller guards it yet.

- source_spec: `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/spec-8-5-marker-deletion-as-a-sanctioned-opt-out.md`
  summary: `clear_opt_out` drops a live `managed[]` claim when handed a region that is still PRESENT in the file, and no caller guards it yet.

The cost is that state alone cannot distinguish "markers deleted, claim survives" (must lose the claim) from "markers present, claim survives" (must keep it): they differ only in the FILE, which this pure function never sees and which its frozen `(state, artifact_id, region)` signature cannot be given. ### DW-FU-8-5-6: State can record only one installed region per hybrid artifact, so a derived opt-out covers at most one of an artifact's declared regions and the rest are re-offered for insertion.

- source_spec: `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/spec-8-5-marker-deletion-as-a-sanctioned-opt-out.md`
  summary: State can record only one installed region per hybrid artifact, so a derived opt-out covers at most one of an artifact's declared regions and the rest are re-offered for insertion.
  evidence: station-unresolved: see the first `8-5` entry's note. Blind Hunter, review pass 2, re-raising as a FUNCTIONAL limit what review pass 1 had already established as a FACT and fixed only in prose. `SeedState.__post_init__` runs `_reject_duplicates` over `managed[].id`, so one artifact carries at most one `ManagedArtifact` and therefore at most one `inserted_region_span` (verified by execution in pass 1). `ManifestEntry` lets an artifact declare several regions, so `detect/optout.py`'s rung 3 can fire for the one claimed region and every sibling falls through to `MISSING` -- and `MISSING`'s shipped remedy re-inserts it. A maintainer who deletes the markers of two regions in one file therefore has one deletion honoured and one silently undone, which is the failure direction FR-112 exists to prevent. NOT fixed in this pass: the fix is a `schema.json` change plus a state migration, both named verbatim in this story's Never bullets ("No new state key, no `schema.json` edit, no state-schema migration"). Pass 1 documented the limit honestly in `record_opt_out` and `detect/optout.py` and retargeted two vacuous tests onto it (`test_state_records_at_most_one_region_span_per_artifact`, `test_the_one_recorded_span_retires_its_region_and_leaves_its_siblings_missing`), so the behaviour is pinned and visible -- what remains is the schema decision itself. ### DW-FU-8-5-10: Rung 3's surviving-marker gate inherits `parse_marker_line`'s canonical-only grammar, so a marker whose inner spacing moved or which gained a non-whitespace line prefix still reads as a deletion and derives a permanent opt-out.

- source_spec: `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/spec-8-5-marker-deletion-as-a-sanctioned-opt-out.md`
  summary: Rung 3's surviving-marker gate inherits `parse_marker_line`'s canonical-only grammar, so a marker whose inner spacing moved or which gained a non-whitespace line prefix still reads as a deletion and derives a permanent opt-out.
  evidence: station-unresolved: see the previous entries' note -- `python3 _bmad/scripts/resolve_config.py --key project` reports `pyforge-mason` from a stale `BMAD_ACTIVE_PROJECT`, while this file's own `readlink -f` `projects/<slug>/` component says `pyforge-marshal`; the disagreement forces the unknown-station id shape (identical to marshal's own). Blind Hunter, review pass 4, confirmed by execution. `seed/detect/optout.py::_marker_region_names` is rung 3's "the markers are GONE" test, and it asks `regions/markers.py::parse_marker_line`, which GUARANTEES recognition of the exact canonical single-space grammar and nothing else -- `_strip_delimiters` requires the literal `"<!-- "` / `" -->"` shape and returns `None` ("ordinary content") for anything else, so a non-canonical marker line is invisible to that gate AND to `parse_regions`. Rung 3 then reads a live, plainly-visible region as a deletion, classifies it `opted-out`, and `opt_outs_to_record` hands the pair over for PERMANENT recording; `record_opt_out` drops the `managed[]` claim and its `body_sha` with it, after which a later repair of the spacing makes `check_managed_region` report HARD `managed-region-modified` forever while `build_plan` plans no insertion to rebuild the claim. Verified by execution: for a `tiers` region fully present with markers and body, `parse_marker_line` returns `None` for a trailing space, a leading indent, a `>` blockquote prefix, and `<!--marshal-seed:begin ...-->` (inner spaces removed). PARTIALLY fixed in review pass 4: each line is now asked twice, raw and `str.strip()`ed, which closes the leading/trailing-whitespace variants (four parametrized regression tests; confirmed by reverting the second ask and watching all four fail). Re-asking the same grammar after whitespace normalization is what `markers.py` says S-8.2 will do wholesale, so it is not a second spelling of the grammar. NOT fixed: the inner-spacing and non-whitespace-line-prefix variants, which need a genuinely looser grammar. That grammar is S-8.2's declared surface -- `parse_marker_line`'s own docstring states that a line whose delimiter spacing varies is unspecified and that "recovering a hand-edited or otherwise non-canonical marker predictably is a future story's job (S-8.2), which re-normalizes a file before consulting this grammar" -- and hand-writing one inside `optout.py` is forbidden by this story's Always bullets ("asked through `markers.parse_marker_line`, never a hand-written substring or regex"). `regions/markers.py` is not in this story's Code Map. The residual is bounded and non-silent in one direction only: over-detecting a surviving marker merely re-offers the region, so the fix, whenever it lands, can be as liberal as S-8.2 wants without new risk.

### DW-FU-8-5-11: A marker-shaped line in ordinary prose permanently disables derived opt-out for that region, with no diagnostic.

- source_spec: `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/spec-8-5-marker-deletion-as-a-sanctioned-opt-out.md`
  summary: A marker-shaped line in ordinary prose permanently disables derived opt-out for that region, with no diagnostic.
  evidence: station-unresolved: `resolve_config.py --key project` answered `pyforge-mason` while `readlink -f` of the destination puts it under `projects/pyforge-marshal/`, so the station is treated as unknown per the minting procedure (the id shape is the same for both branches, and every sibling id here already carries it). Confirmed by execution during review pass 5. `detect/optout.py::marker_region_names` asks `markers.parse_marker_line` of each line twice, raw and `str.strip()`ed, so rung 3 stands down whenever any marker line for the region survives. That normalization is what closes the trailing-space and indent variants, and it is deliberately conservative -- but it also normalizes a marker EXAMPLE written inside an ordinary four-space-indented Markdown code block straight into recognition, and `parse_regions` skips exactly such lines by design. So an artifact whose managed region documents the marker grammar in an indented block carries its own region name in `marker_region_names` on every run, and rung 3 can never fire for it: deleting those markers reports DRIFT `managed-region-missing` and is re-inserted on every `update`, forever, with nothing telling the operator why FR-112 is not being honoured there. The direction of the trade is right (the alternative, under-detection, silently retires a LIVE region and drops its `body_sha`), so this is a residual rather than a regression to revert -- and it is the OPPOSITE residual to `DW-FU-8-5-10`, which tracks the under-detection half. A real fix needs a scan that distinguishes a marker line from a rendering of one -- fence- and indent-awareness `regions/parse.py` already has and `parse_marker_line` does not -- which is the looser grammar `parse_marker_line`\s own docstring assigns to S-8.2. `regions/markers.py` is not in this story's Code Map, and hand-writing a second grammar in `optout.py` is an explicit Always-bullet violation.

### DW-FU-28-3-8: Index freshness is a HEAD-timestamp comparison, so EVERY new commit marks the index stale — in a loop worktree that commits constantly, an enabled `structure-graph` layer sits in near-continuous `kit-item-stale` DRIFT.

- source_spec: `planning-artifacts/specs/spec-28-3-genesis-seeds-the-token-economy-kit.md`
  summary: Index freshness is a HEAD-timestamp comparison, so EVERY new commit marks the index stale — in a loop worktree that commits constantly, an enabled `structure-graph` layer sits in near-continuous `kit-item-stale` DRIFT.
  evidence: `detect/kit.py::_codegraph_check` compares the index mtime against `git log -1 --format=%ct` and reports `stale` whenever `index_mtime < head_ts`. The dominant consequence is not the two accuracy bounds noted below but the CADENCE: a bmad-loop / dispatch worktree commits many times per story, and each commit moves HEAD's timestamp past the index's, so the layer re-reports DRIFT after essentially every commit until something re-syncs. `marshal preflight` does re-sync (and the successful-sync mtime stamp added in review keeps that from becoming PERMANENT drift), but nothing re-syncs between preflights — so a long-running story will show `kit-item-stale` on any `marshal seed check` taken mid-run. Secondary, and stated for completeness: uncommitted edits never mark the index stale, and a rebase that rewrites HEAD's timestamp forward marks it stale with no file change. The rule is deliberate — the same deterministic git-timestamp discipline SPEC-marshal-token-economy CAP-13 requires, no working-tree walk, and no possible false GREEN for the case that matters (commits landed, index not resynced). A cadence fix (a commit-count or time-window tolerance, or a post-commit hook that syncs) is a design choice this story deliberately did not make.

### DW-HYGIENE-2026-09-05-1: worktree/branch hygiene lives in an operator script, not in `marshal retire`

- source_spec: `_bmad-output/projects/pyforge-marshal/planning-artifacts/specs/spec-pyforge-marshal/SPEC.md`
  summary: `scripts/worktree_sweep.py` (2026-09-05, dry-run default, `--execute`) classifies every registered git worktree into KEEP / PRUNE / DELETE / PRESERVE-THEN-DELETE / DELETE-WORKTREE-KEEP-BRANCH / INSPECT from four inputs -- clean-and-ancestor-of-main, the owning station's sprint-ledger status for the branch's story key, whether the branch is on origin, and whether a live process has its cwd inside -- and applies the safe verdicts (patches exported under `~/.local/state/pyforge-marshal/worktree-preserve/` first). `marshal retire` (Story 4.10) proposes only branches named by the most recent bmad-loop run of an attached loop home, so it proposed nothing across a fleet that carried 262 registered worktrees and ~600 merged branches. The sweep's rule set belongs behind the marshal verb (`marshal retire --worktrees`, or a `marshal sweep` verb) so the fleet has ONE retirement authority with journaled evidence; the script is the interim home and its rules are pinned by `tests/scripts/test_worktree_sweep.py`.
  evidence: 2026-09-05 shutdown sweep, hand-verified per item: registered worktrees 262 -> 12 (primary, 8 loop homes, 3 INSPECT), local merged branches 360 + 226 deleted, origin merged branches 227 + 178 deleted in explicit-name batches (the 8 `loop/<station>` heads and every `attempt-preserve/*` kept by policy), 29 GB reclaimed; `marshal retire` dry-run reported `proposals: 0` throughout. Never delete `loop/*` on origin: the station heads read as merged into main whenever the homes are idle.
  note: 2026-09-07 (marshal 31.6) -- `multi-repo-git-ops` does NOT cover this wish. Confirmed via `git submodule status` (empty output) and no `.gitmodules` file in the repo root: this repo has no git submodules at all. `multi-repo-git-ops`'s own SKILL.md scopes it to branching/committing/pushing/syncing across a parent repo and its git-submodule service repos, discovered from `.gitmodules` -- a structurally different concern from this wish's KEEP/PRUNE/DELETE worktree and merged-branch retirement heuristics (no submodules, no branch/worktree lifecycle classification in its scope). The coverage question is answered "no"; this does not resolve the wish itself, which stays a future station-verb story per this entry's own summary.
  location: scripts/worktree_sweep.py
  status: open

  verified: 2026-09-08 — still-open — CONFIRMED present and unchanged: `scripts/worktree_sweep.py` exists with the six-way classification the entry describes. ### DW-STATUS-2026-09-08-1: A retired/cleaned loop-home run leaves `marshal status` reporting that station `unknown` forever, because `latest_run_dir` still returns it while its harness snapshot is gone.

- source_spec: `planning-artifacts/specs/spec-pyforge-marshal/SPEC.md`
  summary: A retired or cleaned loop-home run leaves `marshal status` reporting that station `unknown` indefinitely -- `latest_run_dir` still selects it, but `harness.run_status_snapshot` returns None for it, so the whole row degrades via `journal_unreadable`.
  evidence: Diagnosed live 2026-09-08 against pyforge-steward, which `fleet-picture` has reported as "UNKNOWN - 18 left, needs re-spin" with "status unreadable (stale journal)". Traced end to end. `cli/status.py:896` takes `run_dir = latest_run_dir(home, slug)` -- the LOOP HOME's `.bmad-loop/runs/`, not the in-repo dispatch-runs tree -- and `:926` sets `journal_unreadable=True` whenever `harness.run_status_snapshot(home, harness_run_id)` is None. Steward's home had its runs retired on 2026-08-22 (`.bmad-loop/runs/.retired-failed-20260822/` and `.retired-worktrees-20260822/` both present), so the newest surviving entry has no resolvable harness snapshot and the row has degraded ever since. NOT a data-loss problem, and NOT a stale dispatch journal: the dispatch journal itself is complete and well-formed (19 JSONL events, 0 malformed, a full lifecycle ending `dispatch-preserve` with `ok: true`) at `implementation-artifacts/dispatch-runs/pyforge-steward-20260903T135640861Z-9fc8f532/`. Its preserved patch `failed/43.6/changes.patch` is superseded, not lost: Story 43.6 reads `done` in the tracked ledger and its substance is on main (`python = "3.14.*"` on both `python-agent-platform` and `dbgpt-sidecar`, and the 43.6 story spec exists at `main`). The patch no longer applies in either direction simply because main has moved 349 commits since 2026-09-03. Refreshing the loop home (`marshal refresh`, run the same day, fast-forwarded all eight homes to 103b1376d011) did NOT clear it, which rules out staleness of the checkout as the cause.
  location: src/shared/packages/pyforge-marshal/src/pyforge/marshal/cli/status.py:896
  origin: diagnosed during the 2026-09-08 loop-home refresh pass; recorded rather than patched
  severity: medium
  promoted: 2026-09-08 — hand-recorded after live diagnosis
  status: resolved
  note: The consequence is not cosmetic in one respect worth naming -- a station stuck at `unknown` is a station whose liveness `fleet-picture` cannot assert, which is the precondition for the duplicate-dispatch class already recorded against 2026-08-27. The likely fix is for the derivation to fall back to the dispatch journal's own terminal verdict when the harness snapshot is unresolvable, rather than degrading the whole row; that is a change to Marshal's status contract and wants its own story, not an unscoped patch.

  corrected: 2026-09-08 — the ORIGINAL diagnosis above named the retired-snapshot path, and that path is real and is now FIXED (`run_state_retired` + MRS-STATUS-012: a run whose harness id resolved but whose snapshot is gone reports `idle` with a WARN, while `is_run_live` keeps it conservatively live so no destructive guard is weakened). But it is NOT why pyforge-steward reads `unknown`. Reading steward's own newest loop-home run (`.bmad-loop/runs/20260820-140536-988f`) shows the true cause: its journal carries 32 events of bmad-loop's OWN vocabulary (`run-start`, `story-start`, `session-start`/`session-end`, `story-done`, `run-stop`) and NOT ONE `run-launch`/`run-resume` entry, which is the shape `cli/spin.py` writes and the only shape `_gather_run_journal_facts` folds for a launch pid. That run was started by bmad-loop DIRECTLY, not via `marshal spin`. So `launch_pid is None`, the FIRST `journal_unreadable` branch fires, and the home degrades — even though the same journal plainly records a graceful terminal `run-stop` ("2 done, 0 deferred, 0 escalated ... 8 stories remaining"). Marshal only understands runs it launched itself; a harness-native run is opaque to it, which is exactly what "needs re-spin" has been telling us.
  residual: The remaining fix is to recognise a harness-native terminal run. Deliberately NOT done here: `cli/status.py` folds only marshal's own kinds, and teaching it bmad-loop's `run-start`/`run-stop` vocabulary directly would couple the CLI to the harness's journal format, bypassing `HarnessPort` — the seam that already abstracts bmad-loop for exactly this reason. The clean shape is a `HarnessPort` capability ("is this run terminal?") that `_gather_run_journal_facts` consults when no launch pid is recoverable. That is a contract change to Marshal's status surface and wants its own story, as this entry said from the start.

  owned: 2026-09-08 — the residual now HAS its story: **Story 5.11, "A harness-native terminal run reads as finished, not `unknown`"** (`epics.md` Epic 5, FR-196, ledger `backlog`). Its acceptance criteria bind the seam explicitly — the capability lands in `adapters/harness_bmadloop.py`, `cli/status.py`/`core/status.py` learn no bmad-loop journal kind, an unclassifiable run stays `unknown` with `is_run_live` conservatively live, and `pyforge-steward`'s existing home is the acceptance fixture. This entry stays `open` until that story ships; nothing about the diagnosis changed, it just acquired an owner in a ledger-driven view instead of living only in this note.

  verified: 2026-09-12 — Story 5.11 shipped (PR #1102, 2026-09-10; tracked ledger `5-11-...: done`). Confirmed live: `core/status.py`'s `HomeFacts` carries `harness_native_terminal: bool = False` (line 902, docstring names Story 5.11/FR-196 explicitly, distinguishing it from `journal_unreadable` and `run_state_retired`); `_derive_home_state`-adjacent logic at line 1321 branches on `facts.harness_native_terminal` to route a harness-native terminal run through `derive_home_state` instead of degrading to `unknown`. The capability lands exactly where this entry's own `owned:` note said it would (`adapters/harness_bmadloop.py` + `core/status.py`), via `HarnessPort` per the `residual:` note's own stated design (never a direct bmad-loop-journal-kind coupling in `cli/status.py`). **CLOSED.**

### DW-SPRINTPLAN-2026-09-08-1: `sprint_plan.py generate` silently rewrote the operator's `blocked` gate to `backlog` — the fail-OPEN direction — because `blocked` was never in its vocabulary

- source_spec: `planning-artifacts/specs/spec-pyforge-marshal/SPEC.md` (Story 31.4 governs the sprint-planning trio as a marshal spec surface)
  summary: `blocked` is a repo-local story status that the whole fleet treats as the operator's dispatch gate, but the generator that WRITES the ledger did not recognise it. Every `sprint_plan.py generate` classed it illegal and replaced it with the computed default `backlog` — which means "dispatch me". The gate was enforced downstream and erased upstream.
  evidence: |
    Diagnosed and fixed 2026-09-08. `blocked` appeared NOWHERE in
    `.claude/skills/bmad-sprint-planning/scripts/sprint_plan.py`: absent from
    `STORY_RANK` (line 61: only backlog/ready-for-dev/in-progress/review/done)
    and absent from the `HEADER_COMMENT` vocabulary the shipped
    `sprint-status-template.yaml` mirrors. `_merge_status`'s
    `if existing not in rank:` branch therefore fired on every blocked row and
    returned `computed`, which for a story is `backlog` (build_status line 362)
    or `ready-for-dev` when a story file exists on disk. Three further sites
    (`--set` validation, `cmd_status` counting, `cmd_validate`) each tested
    `status not in RANKS[kind]` and would also have reported a legitimate
    blocked row as illegal.

    Downstream, `blocked` is genuinely load-bearing:
    `marshal/core/dispatch_fleet.py:61` has
    `NON_IMPLEMENT_STATUSES = frozenset({DONE_STATUS, "review", "blocked"})`,
    and bmad-loop's own `stories_engine.py` stops a scan on a blocked story
    ("a blocked story cannot be leapfrogged"). So the dispatcher enforced a
    gate the generator destroyed.

    LIVE DAMAGE. Commit `be0a29b320` (PR #1077, `plan/bmad-suite-lifecycle-2026-09-06`)
    ran a regenerate and flipped FOURTEEN deliberately-blocked `pyforge-steward`
    Epic-44 stories to `backlog` in one sweep — including `44-3-open-the-foundry`
    (creates a GitHub repository), `44-9-mason-submits-to-conda-forge` (opens
    upstream PRs) and `44-10-archive-local-recipes` (outward, irreversible:
    disables CI and archives a repository) — the three that steward's own
    `epics.md` marks "held `blocked`; dispatched only on the operator's explicit
    confirmation, never by a drain" (`fnd:AD-9`). That commit's message documents
    exactly ONE intended flip, "steward 45-2 blocked -> backlog"; the other
    fourteen were collateral, and their fourteen "illegal status" warnings went
    unread alongside a DIFFERENT sprint_plan.py defect found the same session
    (the 80-column yaml wrap, folded into Story 31.4). Blocked-count history on
    the steward ledger: 15 / 15 / 15 through 2026-09-05, then 0.

    Fleet-wide, exactly ONE blocked row survived to 2026-09-08 —
    `pyforge-marshal`'s `31-6-bmad-os-gh-triage-and-multi-repo-git-ops-are-marshal-wielded`
    — one regenerate from the same fate.
  location: .claude/skills/bmad-sprint-planning/scripts/sprint_plan.py:61
  origin: found while verifying whether a scoped steward spin was safe (carry-over pass from PR #1086)
  severity: high
  promoted: 2026-09-08 — hand-recorded at the time of the fix
  status: resolved
  resolution: |
    FIXED in the same pass, not deferred. `STICKY_STATUSES = {"story": frozenset({"blocked"})}`
    names the out-of-lattice statuses; `_is_sticky`/`_is_legal`/`_legal_statuses`
    express legality as "the rank table PLUS the sticky set"; `_merge_status`
    returns a sticky existing status untouched via a guard placed BEFORE the
    `not in rank` branch, and records it in a new `preserved_sticky` report key;
    the three legality sites now call `_is_legal`. `blocked` is documented in
    both `HEADER_COMMENT` and `sprint-status-template.yaml` (a meta-test asserts
    the two never drift). The 14 steward rows were restored to `blocked`, with
    `44-13-memlog-fidelity` left `backlog` — the operator's deliberate first flip
    of 2026-09-04, which must NOT be reverted.

    Proven both directions against the real artifacts, not just by reading:
    the PRE-fix generator (`git show HEAD:...`) run on the RESTORED steward
    ledger destroyed all 14 rows again (`blocked` count 14 -> 0, with 44.3/44.9/
    44.10 back to `backlog`), reproducing the incident exactly; the fixed
    generator preserved all 14 with zero illegal warnings, and independently
    preserved marshal's own `31-6` row. 41/41 existing sprint_plan tests pass.
  note: |
    The class, not just the instance, is worth naming: this is the THIRD
    regeneration data-loss defect found in this one file (after `1aeb911b3b`,
    where a 60-char slug truncation orphaned 13 done steward keys, and
    `6ba6bd9eb6`/Story 31.4's 80-column yaml wrap). All three share a shape —
    a generator that silently discards state it does not recognise — and all
    three were found only after the damage landed. Story 31.4's spec-surface
    governance of the sprint-planning trio exists precisely to catch the next
    one; this entry is evidence that the surface earns its keep.

    An upstream `bmad-method update` will clobber this patch along with the two
    before it. That risk is accepted and pre-existing (the file already differs
    from upstream on two counts); Story 31.4's surface is what detects the
    clobber.

  verified: 2026-09-08 — resolved-in-pass — fix, restore, and both-direction proof landed together.
